newsitem.title: LEBANON: South Lebanon shells leave Sidon residents fearful.
newsitem.headline: South Lebanon shells leave Sidon residents fearful.

text.p: Sidon, once dubbed "the shelter" of volatile south Lebanon, on Tuesday buried victims of a shelling attack as throngs of bewildered mourners expressed rage and fears of further violence.
About 3,000 men marched along the streets of this normally tranquil port city chanting anti-Israeli slogans in a funeral procession.
Many struggled to make sense of the shelling by pro-Israeli militia forces which killed seven civilians on Monday.

Lebanese militiamen led by pro-Israeli Christian commander Antoine Lahd shelled the port after a roadside bomb blew up a car killing two teenage children of a Lahd aide who himself died in a similar blast four years ago.

The shelling marked the bloodiest attack on the Sidon area since Israel's 17-day offensive in the south last year dubbed "Operation Grapes of Wrath", in which about 200 Lebanese civilians were killed.

The 16 shells that landed in Sidon and its suburbs on Monday shattered the local belief that residents were safe from bloody clashes, rocket attacks, air raids and roadside bombs that grip other parts of south Lebanon --the last active Arab border frontline with Israel.
Among the victims of the shelling attack was Riad Firhal, a two-month-old boy who died overnight from wounds caused by shrapnel from one of the shells. His mother died in Monday's attack.
On Tuesday, Sidon hospital officials said the victims also included three Palestinians and a Syrian who were long-time residents of Sidon.
Four people were buried in Sidon, which observed a general strike on Tuesday to remember the dead. Three were laid to rest in the southern city of Tyre.
Israel has distanced itself from Monday's violence, in which at least nine civilians died.

But the line between Israel and its local militia allies was blurred by anger as an Israeli flag was burned and the crowd, which included local officials and pro-Iranian Hizbollah members, screamed anti-Israeli slogans.
"We were born to die while fighting the enemies of God," they chanted.
Residents expressed fear that the city would be trapped in the vicious cycle of attack and reprisal that has killed more and more civilians in the south in recent months.
"Just when we thought we had become human beings, they (the Israelis) are telling us: 'You are just southerners who deserve to live in fear'," said Hani Jardali, a pharmacist.
"It was a quick and brutal trip back to the past. The old black days are back," said Abdel Rahman Jaradi, 25.

Monday's shelling triggered a violent response from the pro-Iranian Hizbollah which claimed responsibility for dozens of Katyusha rockets which hit northern Israel early on Tuesday, wounding at least one civilian and causing some damage.
"This is only part of our response. Hizbollah fighters cannot stand to have their hands tied against these crimes," said Hizbollah parliamentarian Mohammad Fneish, who attended the Sidon funeral.

Hizbollah (Party of God) is fighting to oust Israeli troops and their South Lebanon Army (SLA) militia allies from a 15-km (nine mile) deep Israeli occupation zone set up inside Lebanon with the declared aim of preventing guerrilla attacks on northern Israel.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu warned Hizbollah on Tuesday that his country would retaliate for attacks on civilian lives -- the kind of tough talk which leaves many Sidon residents wondering if another round of shells will strike anytime soon.
"We feel that Sidon is no longer safe," said Khalid Shraidi, a merchant. "A shell might hit anytime now."
